# Initial beta release This is the first beta release of Splunk App for Secure Networking. It provides Cisco-focused dashboards, configurable workspaces, and investigation tools in Splunk Enterprise. ## Highlights - Organizes secure networking content around Zero Trust Access, Secure Infrastructure, Scalable Network Segmentation, Hybrid Mesh Firewalling, and Agentic Ops. - Includes 16 Cisco-themed Dashboard Studio views for executive insights, network and security operations, infrastructure health, workplace intelligence, and investigations. - Provides configurable Insights Workspaces with KPI tiles, layouts, signal rails, connectivity maps, themes, and audience-specific views. - Includes Dashboard Manager tools for creating, editing, cloning, exporting, and presenting dashboards. - Adds interactive topology tools, drilldowns, Open in Search actions, and a searchable catalogue of shared searches. ## Setup and data readiness - Guides users through supporting-app validation, Cisco source-type discovery, index-macro configuration, and data-model acceleration checks. - Supports macro configuration for Cisco networking, security, observability, infrastructure, and workplace integrations. - Includes an in-app User Guide for setup, dependencies, performance readiness, and troubleshooting. ## Beta considerations - This release is available only to approved beta participants. - The app visualizes data already indexed in Splunk Enterprise; it does not collect Cisco data. - Dashboard results depend on the integrations, source types, fields, data models, index mappings, permissions, and time ranges available in each environment. - Features, content, and compatibility can change before general availability.


Short Description:
Alpha (invite only; access requests are not currently being accepted; general availability targeted for fall 2026) — configurable executive, IT operations, and secure networking dashboards unifying Cisco network health, identity, security, infrastructure, application, and topology data in Splunk.


Description:
Alpha release: Participation is by invitation only and limited to a small group of approved users. The app is not yet publicly downloadable on Splunkbase, and access requests are not currently being accepted. General availability is targeted for fall 2026. Splunk App for Secure Networking helps organizations turn fragmented Cisco infrastructure, networking, identity, security, application experience, and building telemetry into clear executive and operational insights in Splunk. Cisco environments often produce data across multiple products, add-ons, indexes, sourcetypes, and data models. Building a consolidated view normally requires teams to create and maintain separate searches, dashboards, index mappings, and visualizations. This app provides a reusable foundation that brings those signals together through configurable dashboards, shared search definitions, index-mapping macros, health indicators, drilldowns, and interactive topology views. The app includes Secure Networking Posture dashboards covering Zero Trust Access, Secure Infrastructure, Scalable Network Segmentation, Hybrid Mesh Firewalling, and Agentic Operations. It also provides executive briefing, IT health, security, asset inventory, network readiness, building intelligence, Cisco Spaces, and network topology experiences. Searches use configurable index macros instead of hardcoded index names, allowing the app to adapt to different Splunk environments. Administrators can use the included Macro Index Tuning utility to discover relevant data and map dashboards to their indexes. Splunk App for Secure Networking does not collect Cisco data directly. It visualizes data already ingested into Splunk through applicable Cisco add-ons, integrations, and data models. The dashboards displayed and populated in each environment depend on the available data sources. The app is intended for network operations, security operations, IT operations, Splunk administrators, architects, customer success teams, and executives who need a consolidated view of the health, security, availability, and performance of their Cisco environment.

item.title: Riskability - v0.1.42 [New App Release]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
# Riskability 0.1.42 Everything since 0.1.33. Four of these change whether the app reports the truth, so they are first. The rest is a new evidence layer on the ATT&CK page and the work that makes a thousand-host fleet affordable. ## Upgrade for these **A feed import no longer strands unchanged hosts on the previous feed's verdicts.** An unchanged host sends only a small heartbeat, so its inventory events can be weeks old and still be current. The matcher read a 24 hour window, chosen before heartbeats existed, so after a feed import only hosts that happened to send a full scan that day could be re-matched. The rest stayed on the old feed's answers with nothing anywhere saying so. The window now matches the heartbeat contract. **A host that goes quiet no longer loses its data.** The hourly snapshots of listening ports, containers and loaded libraries replaced their collections wholesale from a seven day window, so a host quiet for longer had its rows deleted and Exposure showed it with nothing listening rather than saying it had not reported. The snapshots now merge: a host that reported is rebuilt from that scan, so a closed port still disappears, and a host that did not report keeps what it had. A host that has genuinely gone is retired by the age of its last scan, not by the age of these rows. **An uninstalled package now closes its findings.** The inventory state snapshot took the latest version seen in thirty days, so a package the newest scan no longer lists kept supplying a version, went on looking installed, and its findings never closed. **The pipeline no longer marks work done that nobody did.** The checkpoint stamped its own run time rather than the match run, which put every host permanently on the wrong side of a five minute tolerance: the catch up fold reprocessed the entire fleet every hour, and the finding lifecycle took a fallback path that can mark a finding removed. A host the matcher could not reach also had its checkpoint advanced as if it had been handled; it now stays in the queue until a receipt proves it was matched. ## New: the ATT&CK page argues from evidence **Known-exploited CVEs, mapped to the technique that exploits them.** The existing chain infers that a weakness class could enable a technique. This release adds MITRE's Center for Threat-Informed Defense mapping of each CISA known-exploited CVE to the technique that actually exploits it, with MITRE's own sentence on how. It is a recorded fact about a specific CVE rather than a class inference, and it reaches 87 techniques the weakness chain cannot. A new panel draws these techniques against the five reach classes and colours each cell by whether this copy answers the network, not by count, so one known-exploited package on a listening port is as loud as a thousand that answer nothing. Clicking a cell opens the findings behind it, with the CVE linking on to the encyclopaedia. The panel says plainly that it is a floor, covering only the KEV CVEs MITRE has mapped so far, and when the confidence filter is hiding a known-exploited finding an amber callout counts what is hidden and says how to see it. **How an attacker would use this here.** CAPEC's own words, previously discarded, now ship in the feed: the prerequisite an attacker needs and the first move, for each attack pattern the fleet's findings enable. The table keeps the measured reach on the left and MITRE's generic rating on the right, so a scary rating on something unreachable never outranks a reachable finding. **One control, many techniques.** MITRE's mitigations now ship in the feed, and a ranked bar shows how many of the fleet's reachable techniques each control would address, split by reach, so the highest-leverage control comes first. It says what it is: a mitigation reduces the technique, it does not patch the CVE. **The matrix stops colouring techniques that cannot run here.** Each technique now carries the operating systems it can run on, and a host's matrix drops a technique that names none of that host's. On a Linux host that removes 31 Windows and macOS only techniques the mapping was asserting against a machine where they cannot execute. Techniques that name no host operating system, the reconnaissance and cloud ones, are never dropped. The technique table gains a Runs on column. **The page explains its own limits.** The Confidence filter is finally described where it lives: it is about product identity rather than severity, Linux package identities make high confidence and Windows display-name identities make low, so the default view is mostly the Linux fleet. The matrix says how many techniques its size cap is hiding instead of hiding them silently, and the banner states the ceiling nobody had written down: the weakness chain can only ever speak about a quarter of ATT&CK, because MITRE has mapped 167 of 697 live techniques, and the other 530 are not techniques a fleet is safe from. **The drilldown reads like a finding, not a taxonomy.** The findings table behind a technique now leads with the CVE, what it actually is, severity and EPSS, and says that the technique is two steps removed from the CVE and is the category rather than the finding. ## Faster at a thousand hosts **The rare records get their own index.** The collector's heartbeat, exposure, container and link records are 0.98 percent of the inventory index; packages are the rest. The jobs that want only the rare types were parsing a hundred events to keep one. Those types now route at index time to a new index, riskability_meta, kept for a year because a stable host's newest exposure record can be months old and still be the current truth. **Silent truncation is gone from the closing path.** The acknowledgement derived its counts through a join whose subsearch read the whole findings state, which crosses Splunk's sixty second subsearch cap near five hundred hosts and finalises with a partial count and no error. It now reads a small per-host rollup written at fold time. The daily re-match floor is also spread across the day by host name instead of re-matching the whole fleet in the same hour. ## To light the new panels Rebuild the feed with the --mitre flag and import it. The KEV mapping, the CAPEC prose and the mitigations are new feed members, so a bundle built before this release still imports cleanly and the new panels state that they have no data until a rebuilt bundle arrives. Update TA-riskability on your forwarders and TA-riskability-indexes on your indexers, and restart both tiers: the routing to riskability_meta happens at index time, on whichever tier parses. The new index ships in both the app and the indexer add on. A site using its own index names sets the new name in the riskability_index_meta macro and in the routing rule's FORMAT in the add on's transforms.conf, which cannot read a search head macro because it runs on the forwarder.


Short Description:
Correlate the software your fleet already reports against offline CVE databases on a search head with no internet access. Ranks findings by exploitation likelihood and by whether the network can actually reach them. Makes no outbound connections, ever.


Description:
Most vulnerability tooling cannot run where it is needed most. A search head with no route to the internet cannot call an API, pull a feed on a schedule, or fetch a score on demand. Riskability is built for exactly that machine. It takes the software inventory your hosts already report, correlates it against vulnerability databases you carry across the air gap yourself, and answers the question a CVE count never answers: of everything found, what should somebody actually do tonight? THE PROBLEM A fleet of any size produces tens of thousands of open findings. Severity alone does not reduce that to a working list. CVSS describes how bad a vulnerability would be if exploited, not how likely anyone is to exploit it, and neither number knows whether your copy of the software is reachable at all. WHAT THIS APP ADDS Exploitation likelihood. Findings are ranked by EPSS, the published probability that a vulnerability will be exploited in the wild, and by the CISA KEV catalogue of vulnerabilities already observed under exploitation. Both arrive in the feed you import. Neither is fetched live. Reachability. The collector reports listening ports, the process holding each one, and the containers behind them. Riskability uses that to separate findings that answer a network address from those that answer only loopback, and from those with nothing listening at all. On a test fleet of two hosts that turns 10,206 open findings into 11 that answer the network. It reorders the work. It never shortens it, and an unreachable vulnerability is still reported in full. WHAT IT REFUSES TO GUESS Every finding carries a confidence level, and confidence describes the strength of the evidence rather than the severity of the vulnerability. Ubuntu and Red Hat backport fixes without changing the upstream version, so a version comparison alone cannot settle whether such a package is patched. Riskability reports that as informational and says why, rather than asserting a vulnerability it cannot prove. Windows software carries no package identity, only a display name and a registry version, so every Windows finding is reported at low confidence. A Coverage dashboard lists what the feed cannot speak to at all, because a gap in visibility is not the same as an absence of risk. Accepted risks are recorded in an audit index that is written once and never rewritten, holding who accepted the risk, when, the justification, and the date the acceptance expires. NO OUTBOUND NETWORK ACCESS The app makes no outbound requests. You build a feed bundle on a connected machine using the builder the app itself hands you, carry it across, and import it. Nothing is scheduled at install time and nothing reaches the internet on its own.

item.title: Vectra XDR Technology Add-on - v2.0.0 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
## Version 2.0.0 **Important — action required after upgrading.** Data inputs configured in v1.1.2 or earlier will no longer be listed on the Inputs page after this upgrade and must be recreated. Configured accounts, credentials and add-on settings are retained and do not need to be re-entered. ### Breaking change: modular input types renamed All modular input types are now prefixed with `vectra_rux_`: | Previous (v1.1.2 and earlier) | v2.0.0 and later | | --- | --- | | `entity_scoring_input` | `vectra_rux_entity_scoring_input` | | `detections_input` | `vectra_rux_detections_input` | | `audits_input` | `vectra_rux_audits_input` | | `lockdown_input` | `vectra_rux_lockdown_input` | | `health_input` | `vectra_rux_health_input` | Earlier releases used generic input-type names that other Splunk technology add-ons can also define. Modular input names are unique per Splunk instance, so where another add-on defined the same name, Splunk could load the wrong input definition or return an error on the Inputs page. Prefixing every Vectra input type guarantees these definitions are unique. Splunk treats the renamed types as new inputs, which is why data inputs created in v1.1.2 or earlier are not carried forward. ### New features * **Detection input** — added `Include Triaged`, `Include Info Category` and `From Checkpoint ID`. `From Checkpoint ID` lets collection begin from a specific detection event ID on the first run. * **Health input** — added optional collection of EDR and external connector health data: `Get Health EDR`, `Get Health EDR Details`, `Get Health External Connectors` and `Get Health External Connectors Details`. Each dataset is ingested with its own `source` value so it can be searched independently. ### Changes * Detection, audit and lockdown collection migrated to Vectra RUX API v3.5. Health and entity scoring collection continues to use v3.4. * Entity scoring collects from the unified `/entities` endpoint using page-based pagination. * The add-on version reported to the Vectra API is now read from `app.conf` at runtime, so it stays accurate across releases. * Refreshed Vectra branding for the app icon and navigation logo. ### Upgrade procedure 1. Record the configuration of each existing data input (name, interval, index and Vectra RUX account). 2. Disable & delete all configured inputs. 3. Install the v2.0.0 package with the **Upgrade app** option selected. 4. Restart Splunk. A restart is required for this release. 5. Recreate each data input from the Inputs page using the values recorded in step 1. Existing checkpoints are preserved. Recreating an input with the same name resumes collection from where it stopped, avoiding gaps and duplicate events. ### Documentation * [Upgrade guide: v1.1.2 to v2.0.0](https://docs.vectra.ai/configuration/response/siem/upgrade-guide-vectra-xdr-technology-add-on-v1.1.2-to-vectra-rux-technology-add-on-v2.0.0) * [Splunk On-Prem integration guide](https://docs.vectra.ai/configuration/response/siem/splunk-siem-vectra-integration-guide-start-here-for-rux) * [Splunk Cloud integration guide](https://docs.vectra.ai/configuration/response/siem/splunk-siem-vectra-integration-guide-start-here-for-rux-1) ### Support Email [support@vectra.ai](mailto:support@vectra.ai)

The Vectra AI App enables the security operations team to consume the industry's richest threat signals spanning public cloud, SaaS, identity and data center networks inside of Splunk. Short Description:
Convert AWS CloudTrail saved-search alerts into chronological investigation timelines with normalized context, MITRE mapping, entity pivots, manual searches, and exportable evidence.


Description:
EventTimeline turns AWS CloudTrail alerts from Splunk saved searches into structured, chronological investigations. When a saved search triggers, EventTimeline creates a normalized finding containing the alert context, actor, resource, source IP, account, API action, severity, and event timestamp. Analysts can then fetch related CloudTrail activity for a selected investigation window and review what happened before, during, and after the alert. EventTimeline includes chronological evidence views, MITRE ATT&CK and kill-chain context, identity and resource pivots, raw-event access, timeline filtering, Markdown export, a manual timeline generator, and timeline health diagnostics. The app does not include proprietary detection content or require an AI provider. It works with your existing CloudTrail saved searches and allows teams to retain control over their detection logic and investigation workflow.

Description:
DV AI Assistant is an AI-powered security operations application for Splunk designed to help SOC teams investigate security events, generate and execute SPL, and triage Splunk Enterprise Security notable events. The application provides an AI Command Center for natural-language interaction with Splunk data and an AI Triage Center for manual or autonomous notable-event analysis. It supports multiple LLM providers including Ollama, OpenAI, Google Gemini, and custom endpoints, and can use a configurable knowledge base to provide environment-specific context to the AI. DV AI Assistant includes security controls for AI-generated actions and searches. Generated SPL is passed through guardrails before autonomous execution to prevent write or side-effecting commands. IP block and unblock actions require explicit confirmation and the block_ip capability. Built-in admin and sc_admin roles receive this capability by default, while the dv_ai_action role can be assigned separately when block/unblock permission is required. Blocked IP addresses are maintained by the application and exported as a plain-text firewall-consumable list, allowing external firewalls or security controls to retrieve the current block list. The application also includes an autonomous triage worker. When Auto Triage is enabled, the scripted input runs every 60 seconds by default, identifies eligible unprocessed Splunk ES notable events, sends the complete event context for AI analysis, and writes the resulting triage report back to the notable event. Role-based access is provided through dv_ai_user, dv_ai_admin, and dv_ai_action roles. Standard users can access AI Chat and AI Alert Triage, while administrative configuration areas such as AI Providers, Data Context Mapping, Audit, and App Settings are restricted to authorized administrators.

item.title: Adjutant AI (AI Workbench) - v2.4.0 [New App Release]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
# Adjutant AI (formerly AI Workbench) — Release notes What's new, improved, and fixed in each release, in plain language. This is the **customer-facing** summary used for the Splunkbase release-notes section; the full technical changelog lives in the project's detailed release notes. **Last updated:** 2026-08-26 > **About version numbers.** Releases once numbered 0.10–0.13 were renumbered to > 1.0–1.3 to reflect production maturity — no behaviour changed. The current release is > **2.4.0** — a connectivity release on top of **2.2.2**, itself a maintenance release on **2.2.1**, itself a maintenance release on > **2.2.0**'s **Explain a SPL search**, and **2.1.0**'s **Fraud capability** and the **2.0 line** (the deterministic **ITSI Root > Cause Analysis** engine, **resource-consumption monitoring**, and **2.0.7**'s durable memory, > Scheduled Ask and governed integrations), which in turn built on > **1.8.5** (the **CIM Coverage Audit**), **1.8.4** (async playbook execution over MCP > plus the **Outcome Ledger** executive/audit dashboard), **1.8.3** > (a security‑hardening release: OWASP + dependency + anti‑ransomware audit), **1.8.2** (Splunk > Edge Processor data‑quality awareness and keyless Azure OpenAI authentication), **1.8.1** > (support‑diagnosis fixes) and **1.8.0** (agent telemetry & OCSF export, content packs, > all‑tiers data‑quality checks, Splunk 10.x readiness, Dashboard Studio version‑awareness). The > **1.7.0** ServiceNow integration and the **1.5.0 "Data Foundation & MCP OAuth"** themes are > included below. --- ## 2.4.0 "Getting connected" Everything here came out of two customer setups in the same fortnight: an Azure OpenAI service published through a corporate API gateway, and one behind a private endpoint. Both stalled in the same place. The credentials were right, the firewall was open, the built-in connection test was green — and every question still failed. The release is about closing the distance between "the test passes" and "it works", and about not making an administrator assemble a URL by hand from three values nobody gave them. ### Find my endpoint (Azure OpenAI) Azure needs the complete address of a deployment, not the address of the service: everything up to and including `/chat/completions`, with the deployment name and an api-version in it. Behind a gateway that address also carries a path prefix chosen by whoever publishes the API. An administrator is typically handed a base URL and expected to work out the other three parts, and getting any of them wrong produces a "Resource not found" that reads like a permissions problem. There is now a **Find my endpoint** button beneath the endpoint field. Give it whatever you were given — often just the hostname — and it works out the rest from the Splunk server itself, then offers to fill in the endpoint, the deployment and the api-version in one click. Where the service lists its deployments, it also shows you every deployment it found together with the model behind each one, which answers a question customers ask constantly: the deployment is named `gpt-4o`, but is that actually what runs? It finds the address by paying attention to *how* each attempt is refused rather than just that it failed. A gateway refusing an address it does not publish answers differently from Azure refusing a deployment name it does not have, and the second kind of refusal proves the rest of the address is already right. When it cannot finish the job it says exactly what is still missing instead of failing vaguely — most usefully "the address and version are confirmed, the deployment name is not", which turns a five-part question for the API team into a one-part question. It also recognises a service that speaks the OpenAI dialect rather than the Azure one, and tells you to change provider instead of leaving you to guess. It runs only when you press it, and it is capped so it cannot flood anyone's gateway. ### Test connection now reports on the address, not just the login The connection test could report success on a configuration that no question would ever work against. It checked whether the credential was accepted, and an address that answers "not found" still accepts a credential — so a wrong address passed the test and failed every time it was used. That combination sent at least one administrator hunting through firewall rules for an afternoon. It now reports the two things separately. When the address does not work it says so plainly, and distinguishes the two reasons — an address that was left as the service base, or a deployment name that does not exist. When everything is right, it names the model that answered. ### Proxy exceptions, per configuration Reaching Microsoft to sign in and reaching the AI service are two different destinations, and in a locked-down network they often need opposite treatment: the corporate proxy is the only way out to Microsoft, while the service itself answers only on a direct connection. Until now a configuration had one proxy setting for both, so whichever you chose broke the other, and the only workaround changed proxy behaviour for every Splunk process on the machine. Configurations that use a proxy can now list the hosts that must bypass it. Sign-in goes through the proxy, the AI service is reached directly, nothing else on the server is affected, and the change takes effect when you save rather than when you restart. ### Fixed - **Model discovery found nothing behind an API gateway.** The lookup rebuilt the address from the hostname alone and threw away the path prefix, so it asked the wrong place and quietly reported no models. It now keeps the prefix. - **Deployments with your own naming lost their cost figures.** A deployment named for your estate rather than for the model — `acme-gpt4o-prod` — is not a name the price list knows, so usage was recorded with no money against it. The model that actually answered is now recorded alongside the configured name and used for pricing when the configured name is unknown, so those deployments cost correctly. Where the two differ, both are kept. - **A licence that could never be activated said "re-activate".** A key issued with no device limit records no activations at all, so a node-locked tier can never be satisfied by it and pressing re-activate cannot help. The licence page now says the key was issued without a device limit and needs reissuing, instead of sending administrators round a loop that had no exit. --- ## 2.2.2 "Finish the dashboard" A maintenance release about one thing: runs that did all the work and then ended with nothing on the glass. Every item came from watching real dashboard builds on a live estate, and in each case the assistant's own safety check was the reason the dashboard never appeared. The check was right about the problem and wrong about what to do next — it refused, gave instructions, and the instructions either could not be carried out or cost more of the run's budget than was left. ### Fixed - **Dashboards that were refused are now repaired instead.** When two panels ran the same underlying search, the assistant used to stop and describe a three-step manual fix. The fix is mechanical, so the builder now performs it: it creates the shared search once, points both panels at it, and keeps the fields those panels need. Your dashboards get the efficient shape without the run being interrupted, and the same search no longer runs twice. - **Panels that came back empty next to a search that clearly had data.** When a shared search was widened more than once to serve different panels, each widening discarded the previous one. On one nine-panel dashboard five panels showed "No results found" while the search behind them returned the right events. The widenings now combine. - **A check that asked for the impossible.** A panel that calculates its own value — a formatted date, a derived score — was refused for not finding that value in the shared search, where it cannot exist, because the panel computes it afterwards. Values a panel makes for itself are no longer demanded of the search. The related guidance was also wrong in a way that mattered: panels sharing a search are siblings, not a sequence, so a value one panel calculates is invisible to the others and has to be calculated where all of them can see it. - **A failed publish threw away the work it told you to fix.** The message on a validation failure said the dashboard was still open for editing and warned against starting over. It had in fact been discarded, so the repair failed and the assistant rebuilt every panel from scratch — which on one run quietly changed a correct detection into a different one. The dashboard now genuinely stays open when publishing fails. - **One special character could cost an entire dashboard.** A "≥" written as `≥` in a panel's explanatory text made the whole dashboard invalid, discarding a run of around forty steps that had already produced four working searches. Special characters in text are now handled safely no matter which one is used. - **An empty shared-search reference was treated as a real one**, producing a confusing refusal at publish time that asked for a search with a blank name. ### Improved - **Detections are now held to what you asked for.** New guidance covers the ways a detection can look perfect and point at the wrong event — quietly matching a wider set of events than you described, being loosened until it finally returns a row, discarding the field that distinguishes one event type from another, or dropping the amounts and account numbers an analyst needs before the result reaches the table. A rule that renders beautifully and flags the wrong event is worse than one that returns nothing, because nothing looks broken and nobody checks. The assistant now reads its own result back against the raw events before handing it to you. - **"No results" is no longer accepted as proof a detection works.** For a rule whose job is to match something, an empty result proves only that the syntax is valid — "this does not happen in your data" and "this rule cannot detect it" look identical. The assistant now establishes which of the two it is found before telling you, and runs over a period that actually covers the evidence it has already located. - **Sequence detections ("A, then B, then C") are built correctly.** A common shortcut for expressing order silently sorts alphabetically instead of by time, which can make a rule return nothing on a textbook-perfect match. Ordering is now derived from timestamps. ### Changed - **"Create / Update user template" are now "Create / Update user playbook"**, matching the Playbooks tab they belong to. Existing private playbooks you authored are unaffected; the old entries are retired so you are not offered both. --- ## 2.2.1 "Proven" A maintenance release, and every item in it came from running 2.2.0 against a real estate rather than from reading the code. One new capability came along with the fixes. ### Fraud rings your risk threshold cannot see (Enterprise, fraud-analytics) Risk-based alerting adds up one entity's score across many events. A fraud ring is the opposite shape: many entities sharing one thing. Because those are different questions, no amount of threshold tuning finds a ring. Seventeen mule accounts each earning fifteen points against a threshold of forty are seventeen well-behaved customers, since the risk was split seventeen ways and no single account ever crossed. Lower the threshold and you get seventeen false positives, not one ring. This release adds the query that asks the other question: group by the shared attribute instead of by the account. Nothing new has to be collected, because fraud risk rules have always recorded the linking attribute alongside the score. It simply was never read back this way. It is rarity-weighted, which matters more than it sounds. Ask only "what is shared" and the answer is always the corporate proxy that everybody sits behind. Shared attributes are ranked the same way the Fraud Ring Mapper ranks them, so a shared password hash and a shared IP are never treated as equal evidence, and values that are simply infrastructure are shown separately rather than quietly removed — a short list should not be mistaken for a clean estate. It is also honest about one thing it cannot know. It counts accounts that some rule already scored, which is not the same as how many accounts exist that share the value. So it hands you the search that settles it against your real data, and until you run that, it labels its own confidence as provisional instead of guessing. If you cannot name a starting account, the Fraud Ring Mapper will now find candidates for you before it starts walking. ### Fixed - **Money laundering was graded ready on two weeks of data.** Structuring is a run of individually unremarkable deposits and layering is a graph, so neither is visible in a short window however complete the feed is. Our own use case catalogue has always said to grade retention as well as fields; the grader printed that note and never acted on it. History is now graded, and a use case whose data does not go back far enough is capped at partial with the shortfall named. It is worth separating from other gaps, because it is the one you close with a retention policy rather than an onboarding project. On our demo estate this moved money laundering from ready to partial. - **Every ServiceNow tool call failed** with an internal error reference and no explanation. A tenant lookup returned a dictionary and the calling code expected a pair. - **The fraud readiness dashboard.** Four defects, found by running it rather than reading it. The readiness lookup was private to our own app, so when a dashboard was generated into a customer app the summary panel could not resolve it and rendered empty — which reads as "nothing has been graded" rather than "you cannot see it from here". The audit's own verdicts were being re-graded on the way to the screen, so nine computed verdicts became eight different ones. The coverage audit could not reach the dashboard builder at all, so nothing enforced that a panel must return data before it goes on the glass, and an empty panel on a fraud dashboard is read as "nothing wrong". And no fraud dashboard mentioned data quality: no ingestion check, no TrackMe, no Cribl or Edge Processor. A readiness grade computed over a feed that is arriving late or half delivered is a confident answer about the wrong data, and it fails towards "you are ready". That panel is now mandatory and appears even when everything is clean, because "we checked and it is healthy" is a finding. - **Asking for a readiness audit in plain English now reaches the readiness audit.** The question our own demo guide tells people to ask did not route to the playbook it names. - **Fraud verdict columns are coloured.** Ready, partial and blocked — and the feed inventory's present and absent — were missing from the status colour map, so those columns could only be coloured by hand and often were not. - **A dashboard opened from a finished session sat on "Loading..."** until you refreshed the tab. The new tab was sharing a browser process with a page that was still busy, so it never got a chance to start. - **The dashboard builder could refuse a fix it gave no way to make.** A publish refusal asked for a base search to be amended, and nothing could amend one, so the assistant looped between rebuilding and hand-editing. There is now a tool for it. - **The write-confirmation prompt asked about writes that could not succeed.** You were approving changes that validation then refused anyway. Validation now runs first, so the prompt only appears for writes that can actually happen. - **Token and cost accounting missed cached tokens.** With prompt caching the provider reports only the uncached part of the input, so an agentic run showed a few thousand tokens next to a cost that looked impossible. Cached tokens are now recorded, priced and shown. This affected what we reported, never what you were charged. - **Test Connection for Azure could only ever time out on a broken network.** Its own retries outlasted the window Splunk Web allows, so you got a bare 504 instead of the staged diagnostic. It now finishes inside the window and tells you which stage failed. ### Improved - **History groups by conversation.** A playbook run and its follow-up replies were listed as separate entries. They are now one entry with the turns nested inside and a combined cost. - **Large tool results no longer inflate every later call.** A stateless chat API re-sends the whole conversation on each tool round-trip, so one oversized result was paid for repeatedly. Results are now bounded before they enter the conversation. --- ## 2.2.0 "Explain" ### Explain a SPL search — free on every tier Point it at a search and get back an explanation you keep. Paste the SPL, name a saved search, or give it a dashboard and let it explain every panel. You get a private dashboard and a private saved search holding the same search fully commented, using native SPL comments so the commented copy is still a real, runnable search rather than a printout. This is on **every tier, including the free one**. Reading somebody else's search is the first thing a new Splunk user needs and the last thing they should have to pay for. **It explains what the search does here, not what the commands mean in general.** Your macros are expanded to their real definitions. `tag=web` is resolved to the eventtypes it actually selects on your system. Lookups are shown with their real columns. Command behaviour comes from your own installation's grammar, so an app-contributed command is described correctly. **And it runs the thing.** The pipeline is split at up to four points and each piece is executed over your sample window, so the walkthrough says "the base search returns 4,812 events with 14 extracted fields; after `stats count by host, status` that becomes 37 rows with 3 fields" using your real names and numbers. A field the SPL references that never appears in the results is flagged — the most common silent SPL bug, and one no text-only explainer can see. A search that returns nothing is bracketed to the stage where it broke. Nothing it could not verify is presented as if it were. Verified and unverified statements are never mixed together quietly. ### "Explain this" is usually "why did this stop working" Those two questions arrive in the same sentence, and reading SPL cannot tell them apart: a search whose data stopped arriving looks exactly like a search that was always wrong. So every run takes a feed verdict for the indexes involved, whether or not the search looked healthy. A source that stopped reporting half its hosts, or is arriving four hours late, still returns rows and still looks right — that is precisely when a check is worth having. When something does look off it goes further: ingestion parsing errors, Cribl Stream and Edge Processor if they front your indexers, and the CIM layer, where a perfectly written search returns nothing because acceleration has not backfilled or the index is not in the data model's allowlist. All of that is available on every tier. The per-field CIM audit still needs Professional, and when it is not available the dashboard says so in place, naming what that audit would have told you. ### Fixed - **CIM Coverage Audit acceleration check.** Since 1.8.5 it reported "not visible to the data model" for every source on every estate, because of how it referenced the sourcetype field in `tstats`. It now reports the real counts. If you have run a CIM audit before and were told acceleration could not see your data, run it again. - **Generated dashboards.** Splunk rejects malformed markup with the single unhelpful phrase "Invalid XML."; the app now says what is actually wrong and repairs the common cases itself. Panels bound to a shared base search are checked for the field-pruning trap that makes a panel render empty, or show a wrong number, while the same search works fine when opened in Search. --- ## 2.1.0 "Fraud" Splunk's own App for Fraud Analytics reaches end of life on 1 May 2027, and it is not alone: the App for Anomaly Detection retired in 2025, standalone UBA ends in January 2027, and the App for Behavioral Profiling froze at Splunk 9.4. Four packaged analytics apps retiring on one path, and their customers have no answer today. This release is that answer. - **Find out what your data can actually support, in about a minute.** The Fraud Data Coverage Audit reads your real events and tells you which fraud use cases you can run today, which are partial and why, and which are blocked with the feed that is missing named. It works out which of your sources is which by looking at what they CONTAIN, not what they are called, because real sourcetypes never match the documentation. Today this answer takes a workshop and three weeks of a consultant. - **The check nobody else makes.** It measures whether your entity keys actually survive from one feed to the next. Ring detection is the payoff use case and it is the one most often declared ready on the strength of the fields being present, then failing because an account or device cannot be followed across the boundary. It also tells you when a feed carries every field perfectly but only knows about a fraction of your customers, which is a different problem with a different fix. - **Count actors, not accounts.** One person can open many accounts using the fact that Gmail ignores dots, and to your signup system they look like many different people. Adjutant knows to collapse those, and knows NOT to do it for other providers, where merging two customers would invent a fraud ring that does not exist. When it links entities it always shows you how rare the shared attribute is, because a shared IP address means nothing behind a mobile network and a great deal on a home line. - **Scoring that fits where you already are.** If you run Enterprise Security, everything goes into your existing risk framework and nothing parallel is built. If you do not, it uses the same field names anyway, so the day you buy ES you change a destination rather than rewrite your detections. - **Behavioural profiling that outlives the app it replaces.** Describe the behaviour in a sentence and get a working indicator, anomaly rule and ranked entity list. It compares an entity against its own history, or against its peer group, which the retiring app could not do. Short Description:
A workbench for Splunk, not just a chatbot. Analyse, correlate and build across SPL, dashboards, alerts, AI Toolkit / MLTK, ES, ITSI and TrackMe through tools that understand each one — plus any MCP server you add. Pick your LLM: Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure, Groq, Gemini, Bedrock, Ollama, OpenRouter. Multi-tenant, multi-tier (Free, Pro, Enterprise, MSP).


Description:
Adjutant AI (formerly AI Workbench) is a generative workspace for Splunk — not a chatbot bolted onto search, but a real workbench where you investigate, analyse and build with tools that understand Splunk. It is a host shell: it has no use-cases of its own, deriving everything from the Splunk app a user opens it from and their roles. Install once on the Search Head, then embed it in the apps your users already live in — Search, ITSI, Enterprise Security, your SOC and MSP customer apps. Users never leave the app they came from, and artefacts land in that app's namespace. Ask in plain English. Get back validated SPL, Simple XML and Dashboard Studio dashboards, alerts, lookups, reports and Splunk AI Toolkit (MLTK) machine-learning pipelines — grounded in your running Splunk (your knowledge objects, live command syntax, CIM models), run for real before they are saved, owned by the calling user. The depth is the difference. Where a generic MCP-only assistant talks to Splunk through one broad door, Adjutant AI ships fine-grained, Splunk-aware tools across Core, Enterprise Security, ITSI, TrackMe, ServiceNow and the AI Toolkit, each scoped to one job and run under your existing Splunk ACLs. Extend it with HTTP tools or any MCP server. New in 2.1 — a fraud capability that starts by telling you what you cannot yet detect. The Fraud Data Coverage Audit grades your estate against nine use cases (including AML) and returns ready, partial or blocked with the specific blocker, identifying event families by what events contain rather than by sourcetype name. Entity resolution runs before scoring, because risk accumulates per entity. Generated rules are weighted contributions with readable reasons, emitted into Enterprise Security's risk framework where it exists and into RBA's own field vocabulary where it does not. Nothing generated is ever enabled or scheduled. New in 2.0 — ITSI Root Cause Analysis with no LLM in the answer. It walks your real dependency graph, verifies the data behind every KPI, scores the evidence transparently, then lets an LLM narrate. The same evidence always gives the same answer. A red KPI on a dead feed is a data problem, and it names the forwarder, HEC, DB Connect, Cribl or Edge Processor leg at fault. Plus durable memory, scheduled playbooks, governed integrations, and per-tenant resource-consumption reporting. Your SOC can watch the agent: LLM calls, tool and ServiceNow calls, config changes, unattended verdicts and policy refusals emitted as OCSF events to an index Enterprise Security already watches. On-prem, no cloud egress, off by default. Bring your own LLM: Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Groq, Gemini, Bedrock, Ollama (fully offline) or OpenRouter — server-side, so keys never leave the search head. Multi-tenant by design. Free, Professional, Enterprise and MSP tiers, self-serve and air-gap-friendly.

item.title: Mondoo Add-On (TA) for Splunk - v1.0.0 [New App Release]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
## 1.0.0 First public release of the Mondoo Technology Add-on for Splunk. ### Data collection Two independent collection paths, usable together or separately. **Mondoo GraphQL API**, through a modular input polling your Mondoo space on a configurable interval: | Sourcetype | Contents | |---|---| | `mondoo:rest:audit` | Audit trail of actions in your space | | `mondoo:rest:advisory` | Security advisories | | `mondoo:rest:agent` | Registered Mondoo agents | **File-based ETL**, through a file monitor that reads JSONL exports from the Mondoo ETL runner and assigns sourcetypes automatically from the filename: | File suffix | Sourcetype | |---|---| | `-assets.jsonl` | `mondoo:json:asset` | | `-vuln.jsonl` | `mondoo:json:vuln` | | `-checks.jsonl` | `mondoo:json:check` | | `-controls.jsonl` | `mondoo:json:control` | | `-packages.jsonl` | `mondoo:json:package` | | `-queries.jsonl` | `mondoo:json:query` | ### CIM Events are tagged and field-aliased for the Common Information Model, covering the Vulnerabilities, Change, Inventory and Alerts data models. A lookup maps raw Mondoo actions to CIM change types. ### Reliability - Checkpointed, resumable pagination. Restarts resume where collection stopped rather than refetching, and a configurable lookback controls how much history the first run pulls. - Automatic retry with exponential backoff and jitter on rate limits and transient errors, honouring `Retry-After`. - Outbound HTTPS proxy support, and custom CA bundles for networks with TLS interception. - Bearer tokens and JWTs are stripped from every log line the add-on writes, so diagnostic output can be shared safely. ### Configuration Inputs can be created and edited from a setup page inside Splunk Web, or defined directly in `inputs.conf`. ### Dashboards The optional companion app **Mondoo** (`mondoo_app`) adds dashboards for asset inventory, vulnerabilities, policy checks, query coverage and indexing health. All dashboards resolve the index through a single `mondoo_index` macro, so pointing them at a non-default index is a one-line change. ### Compatibility - Splunk Enterprise 9.0 and later. Verified on Splunk 9.3 and 10.2. - Python 3.9 through 3.13. The add-on selects the interpreter Splunk provides. - Requires a Mondoo service account credential. ### Known limitations **Splunk Cloud.** Cloud stacks do not permit custom Python modular inputs in stack apps, so this add-on cannot be installed directly into a Cloud stack. Run it on a heavy forwarder you operate and forward the events in. The `mondoo_app` dashboards install into a Cloud stack without issue. **Single instance only.** The modular input is stateful and keeps checkpoint files locally. Running it in more than one place, including on multiple search head cluster members, produces duplicate events. Run it from one heavy forwarder outside the cluster. **Data models require the CIM add-on.** This add-on supplies CIM tags and field aliases, not the data models. Searches using `datamodel` need the Splunk Common Information Model Add-on installed separately. Tag-based searches work without it. **ETL filename suffixes are exact.** The vulnerability export uses the singular `-vuln.jsonl`, while the others are plural. A file that does not match a known suffix stays on the generic `mondoo:json` sourcetype rather than raising an error.


Short Description:
Ingests security and compliance data from the Mondoo platform into Splunk: vulnerabilities, policy checks, asset inventory, advisories and audit activity. Collects via the Mondoo API on a schedule or from file-based ETL exports, with CIM mappings for the Vulnerabilities, Change, Inventory and Alerts data models.


Description:
Mondoo Log Ingestion (TA-mondoo) brings security and compliance data from the Mondoo platform into Splunk. THE PROBLEM Mondoo continuously assesses your infrastructure for vulnerabilities, misconfigurations and policy violations. That data is valuable, but it lives in a separate console. Security teams end up switching tools to answer basic questions: does this CVE affect a production asset, did a failing control coincide with a change, which hosts drifted out of compliance this week. Correlating Mondoo findings with the logs already in Splunk otherwise means manual exports and spreadsheets. WHAT THIS ADD-ON DOES TA-mondoo collects Mondoo data on a schedule and indexes it in Splunk, so findings sit alongside your existing telemetry and can be searched, alerted on, and built into dashboards and compliance reports. Two collection paths: 1. Mondoo GraphQL API (modular input), polling your Mondoo space on a configurable interval: mondoo:rest:audit - audit trail of actions in your space mondoo:rest:advisory - security advisories mondoo:rest:agent - registered Mondoo agents 2. File-based ETL (file monitor), ingesting JSONL exports from the Mondoo ETL runner, routed to sourcetypes automatically by filename: mondoo:json:asset, :vuln, :check, :control, :package, :query CIM MAPPING Events are tagged and field-aliased for the Splunk Common Information Model, so they populate the Vulnerabilities, Change, Inventory and Alerts data models and work with CIM-based apps and correlation searches. OPERATIONAL DETAIL Checkpointed, resumable pagination, so restarts neither duplicate nor lose events, with a configurable lookback window on first run. Automatic retry with exponential backoff on rate limits and transient errors, honouring Retry-After headers. Outbound HTTPS proxy and custom CA bundle support for restricted networks. Bearer tokens and JWTs are scrubbed from every log line, so diagnostic output is safe to attach to support tickets. Configurable from Splunk Web or directly in inputs.conf. DEPLOYMENT Install on a single instance: a heavy forwarder, or the search head in smaller deployments. The modular input is stateful and writes checkpoint files, so enabling it on more than one search head cluster member produces duplicate events. Requires Splunk Enterprise 9.0 or later and a Mondoo service account. Tested on Splunk 9.x and 10.2. DASHBOARDS The companion app "Mondoo" (mondoo_app) provides prebuilt dashboards for asset inventory, vulnerabilities, policy checks, query coverage and data quality, built on the sourcetypes above. It is optional; the add-on indexes data on its own. Licensed Apache-2.0. Source and issue tracker: https://github.com/mondoohq/splunk-app

Release Notes:
Version 1.0.0 (initial release) First public release of TA-macadress. Adds the macaddresslookup search command, which enriches any event containing a MAC address field using the macadress.com API: \- Vendor and manufacturer identity (organization, OUI, matched registry prefix) \- Device category inference (router, switch, wireless access point, embedded device, and more) \- Virtualization and container detection (VMware, Hyper-V, Xen, VirtualBox, Parallels, QEMU/KVM, Docker's default bridge convention) \- Special-use address classification (broadcast, multicast, VRRP, HSRP, STP, LACP, 802.1X, LLDP) \- Randomization confidence signals for flagging spoofed or privacy-randomized addresses Lookups are batched for efficiency (up to 100 addresses per API call). The API key is entered once via the app's Set up page and stored through Splunk's encrypted storage/passwords endpoint. Requires a free or paid [https://macadress.com](https://macadress.com) API key (https://macadress.com/signup) and outbound HTTPS access from the search head to [https://api.macadress.com.](https://api.macadress.com.)


Short Description:
Add a macaddresslookup search command that enriches any event with a MAC address field: manufacturer, device type, virtualization/container signals, randomization confidence, and reserved/protocol address detection, all in one streaming SPL command.


Description:
TA-macadress adds a `macaddresslookup` search command that resolves MAC addresses to vendor, device category, virtualization, and special-use information, using the macadress.com API. Any event with a MAC address field, DHCP leases, ARP tables, wireless associations, switch port tables, asset inventories, can be enriched in place with: - Vendor and manufacturer identity, resolved against the full IEEE OUI registry (organization name, matched registry prefix, country) - Device category inference (router, switch, wireless access point, embedded device, and more) from a manually curated, source-verified dataset, not a guess - Virtualization and container detection: VMware, Hyper-V, Xen, VirtualBox, Parallels, QEMU/KVM, and Docker's default bridge convention - Special-use address classification: broadcast, IPv4/IPv6 multicast, VRRP, HSRP, STP, LACP, 802.1X, LLDP, each with its source protocol cited - Randomization signals: whether an address is locally administered or otherwise likely to be a privacy-randomized or spoofed MAC, useful for flagging anomalous device behavior in security and asset-inventory use cases This turns a raw MAC address into something you can actually search, filter, and stat on: `stats count by mac_organization`, `where mac_virtualization_platform!=""`, `where mac_potentially_randomized=1`, and so on, without leaving SPL. Lookups are batched (up to 100 addresses per API call) for efficiency on large event volumes, and the API key is stored via Splunk's encrypted storage/passwords endpoint rather than a plain-text configuration file. A free API key is available at macadress.com/signup; paid plans raise the request-rate and monthly-quota limits for larger deployments.

Description:
SPLap is a motorsport telemetry lab for the Splunk platform. Install one package and the 2025 Italian Grand Prix at Monza is already replaying: 20 cars on a circuit map derived from the cars' own GPS, a timing tower, per-driver telemetry traces and deterministic Race Engineer findings, with the SPL behind every panel one click away. No setup, API key, index, internet access or LLM is required to run it. What is inside - Real session data from the community OpenF1 API: 3.7 Hz location and car telemetry (speed, RPM, gear, throttle, brake, DRS), laps, sectors, stints, pit stops, positions, intervals, race control, weather, overtakes and team radio, packaged as gzip lookups and static replay assets. - Canonical schema splap.canonical/1: one index, 17 splap:* sourcetypes with props.conf timestamping, every event tagged observed / derived / modeled / unavailable, a per-session capability object and an idempotent import_id so a session is never indexed twice. - Pit Wall: hybrid SVG + Canvas renderer (circuit, pit lane, curbs, sectors, DRS zones, numbered corners; livery-coloured cars with collision-aware labels), 500 ms replay frames interpolated in the browser, 0.25x-4x replay, jump to pit / overtake / flag, data layers, broadcast mode. Zero searches per animation frame, at most four to load. - Lap Delta: two real laps aligned by distance with per-corner braking point, minimum speed, throttle reapplication and time gained or lost. - Incident Review: a 30-second evidence window around any race-control message, overtake, pit stop or team radio, with map, telemetry, gaps and weather on one cursor. - Race Engineer: deterministic rules with rule version, confidence, provenance, evidence and the SPL that reproduces each finding. No LLM. - Connect Data: import any historical session from the browser, load an offline race bundle, or use the Python CLI with HEC. Credentials never touch browser code. - Install Doctor with 28 executed checks; SPL Garage, Strategy Lab and Labs on a labelled synthetic fixture. Why Splunk: it ingests a hundred thousand telemetry events without blinking, SPL is made for these time-series questions, and Simple XML plus SplunkJS let us draw a race instead of a bar chart. Co-developed by Lloyd Clark and Lilli. We are both big F1 nerds; this started as a father-daughter weekend project to learn how real apps get built and to lay the groundwork for modeling race physics. Version 2.1 is the data foundation; the physics is next. SPLap is an independent project, not affiliated with, endorsed by, sponsored by or certified by Splunk LLC, Formula One Licensing BV, the FIA, any team, driver or circuit. Race data is provided by OpenF1 under its non-commercial terms; no official logos, sponsor graphics or car images are used and team colours are curated approximations.

item.title: Microsoft Windows Firewall Observability - v4.0.0 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
# Release notes ## 4.0.0 **Minimum platform is now Splunk Enterprise / Splunk Cloud 10.4.** Version 3.1.0 stays available on Splunkbase for 9.x deployments and remains supported — 4.0.0 is the same app rebuilt around what Dashboard Studio 10.4 makes possible, not a different product. ### The headline: a segmentation map New **Segmentation Map** dashboard, built on the 10.4 network graph. The firewall log is the cheapest east-west flow evidence most estates have; this turns it into something you can act on. - **Host map** — every host and the peers it reached, edge thickness by flow count, force layout. - **East-west** — Internet traffic removed, so what is left is exactly what a segmentation policy is supposed to constrain. Paired with a table of accepted RDP / SMB / WinRM / SSH / database paths. - **Segments** — addresses grouped by /24, /16 or host, rendered both as a hierarchical graph and as a flow matrix punchcard. Every dot is a path that exists today; every empty cell is a boundary nothing crossed. - **Services** — which protocols actually carry the cross-boundary traffic. Usually a much shorter list than people expect. - **Lateral reach scoring** — how many internal hosts each machine reached, against the estate average in standard deviations, so an outlier surfaces without a hand-tuned threshold. ### Tabs everywhere they replace scrolling Eight of the nine dashboards are now tabbed. Nothing was removed; the same panels stopped being a two-thousand-pixel scroll. | Dashboard | Tabs | |---|---| | Firewall Overview | Summary · Collection health · Geography & changes | | Traffic Explorer | Flow map · Volume · Breakdown | | Segmentation Map | Host map · East-west · Segments · Services | | Host 360 | Activity · Peers & services · Processes · Changes | | Process Attribution | Process map · Hunting · Outbound & listeners | | Firewall Changes | Activity · Posture over time · Actors · Full history | | Threat Hunting | Reconnaissance · Command & control · Exposure · Data movement | | Firewall Posture | Compliance · Blind spots · Rule inventory | Peer Pivot and Traffic Investigator stay single-page on purpose: they are drilldown targets, and a drilldown lands on the first tab. ### More network graphs Beyond the segmentation map, the graph is used wherever a relationship reads better than a table: - **Beaconing map** (Threat Hunting) — hosts and the addresses they call back to. One external node with many host edges is either your management tooling or your incident. - **Exposure map** — which public addresses reach which of your hosts. - **Peer map** (Host 360) and **reach map** (Peer Pivot). - **Process to service map** (Process Attribution and Host 360). - **User to host change map** (Firewall Changes) — an account touching many hosts is either your automation or your problem. - **Host to risk map** (Posture) — which machines carry which rule risks. ### Timelines The 10.2 timeline visualisation, where a lane per category beats a stacked column: - Firewall Changes: change timeline by outcome, and an enable/disable timeline per host — a red mark is a window during which a host was unprotected. - Host 360: change timeline by category. - Threat Hunting: scan activity by intensity band. - Posture: posture drift over time. ### Trellis small multiples - Overview: blocked ratio as one colour-ranged gauge per host — an outlier is visible without reading a table. - Posture: compliance as a filler gauge per firewall profile. Public is usually the one that drifts. - Firewall Changes: change count per severity. - Traffic Explorer: one column chart per verdict. - Process Attribution: blocked events per binary. ### Conditional sections Sections that depend on optional data sources now disappear instead of sitting empty. Panels carry `hideWhenNoData`, and an **Optional sections** input removes their headers too. Affects the process attribution blocks in Host 360 and Threat Hunting, and the live posture panel in Host 360. ### Smaller 10.x touches - Row numbers on every investigation table. - Range-based cell colouring on the columns where a number carries a verdict: beaconing `jitter`, outbound `mb_out`, exposure `sources`, lateral `deviation`, segment `flows`. - Markdown tables in the release-notes-style panels and the documentation view. - Line chart acceleration applies automatically to the high-density time charts. ### Unchanged from 3.1.0 Every macro, field, eventtype, lookup, saved search, data model and view name is identical. The collection layer, the CIM mappings, the detections and the companion **TA-windows-firewall-posture** (still 1.0.0, still Splunk 9.0+, forwarder side) are untouched. Upgrading from 3.1.0 is a package replacement with no reconfiguration. ## 3.1.0 Three things this release is about: knowing **which binary** opened a connection, making the app **survive real data volumes**, and answering **"what is the state right now"** rather than only "what changed while we were watching". ### Added — process attribution - **Process Attribution view**. Windows Filtering Platform audit events (Security 5152/5156/5157, plus 5154/5155/5158/5159 for listeners) carry the full application path that `pfirewall.log` does not have. The app normalises them entirely in SPL, through the new `wfo_wfp` macro, so it never claims props on the shared `XmlWinEventLog:Security` sourcetype and never conflicts with Splunk_TA_windows or your existing Security collection. - New macros `wfo_wfp_index`, `wfo_wfp_base`, `wfo_wfp` and `wfo_network` (unified pfirewall + WFP). - Four detections: LOLBin with network activity, rare binary making network connections, new listening process, process repeatedly blocked outbound. - The setup page now takes a second index, because Security events almost never live in the same index as the firewall traffic log. ### Added — performance - **`Windows_Firewall_Observability` data model**, two datasets (Traffic, Changes), 48 fields. Acceleration ships **off** — that cost is your decision, not the app's. - The Overview now runs on `tstats` against that model. It works either way: with `summariesonly=false` (the shipped default) it searches raw data exactly as before; set the `wfo_summariesonly` macro — or answer "yes" on the setup page — once acceleration is on, and the same page reads summaries only. - New `is_noise` field, computed in props from the fixed non-routable, multicast, broadcast and reserved ranges. Unlike the `ip_whitelist` lookup, it is a data model field, so tstats panels can filter structural noise. The lookup stays as the tuning layer for your own organisation-specific ranges on the raw-search views. ### Added — investigation workflow - **Host 360**: one machine, everything — peers, services, processes, firewall state, configuration history, and its distinct-peer count against its own rolling 24-hour baseline expressed in standard deviations. - **Peer Pivot**: one IP address, everything — how far it reached into the estate, which ports, the timing regularity of the exchanges per host, and which processes talked to it. - Every table across the Overview, Traffic Explorer, Investigator, Threat Hunting and Posture views now drills into Host 360 or Peer Pivot instead of dumping you into a raw search, carrying the time range along. - Navigation regrouped into Traffic / Investigate / Configuration collections. ### Added — posture - **Firewall Posture view** plus the companion **TA-windows-firewall-posture** (separate package, forwarder side). Two read-only PowerShell inputs inventory the profile state, default actions, logging settings, log file health and the enabled rule set with a risk score. - This closes the blind spot the event stream cannot: a host whose firewall was already off before Splunk arrived produces no change event, and a host with drop logging disabled produces no traffic log at all — until now it was indistinguishable from a quiet host. - Four detections, including **Host Not Logging Dropped Packets**, which is the one that tells you an empty dashboard means nothing. ### Notes - Minimum platform is still Splunk 9.0. Dashboard Studio features that would have helped here — network graph, tabs, conditional panel visibility — need 10.x and were deliberately left out. - Nothing from 3.0.0 was removed. Existing macros, fields and view names are unchanged. ## 3.0.0 Major release. Collection, normalisation, dashboards and detections were all reworked. ### Fixed - **The setup page had no effect.** It wrote a macro named `windows_pfirewall_index` while every search of the app used `windows_firewall_index`. Whatever index you configured was ignored and all searches silently ran against `index=*`. Re-run the setup page once after upgrading. - **Field extraction shifted by one column on some Windows builds.** The positional `DELIMS` extraction assumed 18 columns; Windows Server 2016/2019 write 17 (no process id). Replaced by a regex extraction whose last group is optional, so both layouts are handled. - **Data loss after log rotation.** The four header lines of `pfirewall.log` are identical after every rotation, so Splunk computed the same CRC and resumed at the previous offset. `initCrcLength = 2048` now makes the CRC include real traffic lines. - **Header lines were indexed as events**, polluting every count. They are now routed to nullQueue. - Wrong CIM mapping: `protocol` carried the transport value. It now carries the network-layer value (`ip` / `ipv6`); `transport` keeps `tcp` / `udp` / `icmp`. - Profile bitmask decoding only handled Public, Private and None. Domain and the combined values (3, 5, 6, 7, 2147483647) are decoded too. - Typos in the vendor product name ("Windows Defender Firewal"). - The `windows_firewall_event_id` lookup returned up to nine rows for a single EventID, turning `Description` into a multivalue field. It is now one row per EventID. ### Added - **Five Dashboard Studio views**, responsive grid layout, dark theme: - *Firewall Overview* — collection health, allowed vs blocked volume, blocked ratio, noisiest services, top talkers, firewall state per host, world map of external destinations. - *Traffic Explorer* — two-level flow map (host → service → verdict), volume in connections and in bytes, services, remote peers, activity punchcard. - *Traffic Investigator* — filterable tables with geo enrichment and service resolution. - *Firewall Changes* — severity-ranked audit trail, change timeline, authors, firewall state. - *Threat Hunting* — port scans, network sweeps, beaconing, Internet exposure, data movement. - **Sixteen saved searches**: 15 detections (all disabled by default) and 6 reports. Highlights: firewall disabled, default inbound action set to allow, service stopped, policy reset, inbound allow rule created, rule deleted, policy change burst, port scan, network sweep, excessive denied outbound, C2 beaconing, data exfiltration, exposed service, administrative protocol exposed, host stopped reporting. - **Service resolution**: `dest_service` is derived from the destination port and transport through a new lookup of 81 common services. - **Internal / external scoping**: `src_scope` and `dest_scope` let every search separate lateral traffic from Internet exposure. The ranges are configurable from the setup page. - New macros `wfo_traffic`, `wfo_changes` and `wfo_internal_ip(ip)`. - Severity ranking of configuration events (`severity`), plus `firewall_enabled`, `default_inbound_action`, `default_outbound_action` and `setting_name`. - CIM **Change** data model compliance for the configuration events: `action` now uses the allowed set (created / modified / deleted), with `object`, `object_category`, `object_attrs`, `object_path` and `result`. - Optional input stanzas for per-profile log files, the ConnectionSecurity channel and the Windows Filtering Platform audit events. - A rewritten setup page: validation, live feedback, index list and internal ranges, no silent failure. - A rewritten documentation view: installation, GPO and PowerShell activation, field reference, tuning and a troubleshooting table. ### Changed - The generic eventtype `traffic`, which was exported globally, is replaced by `windows_firewall_traffic`. The app extracts IP addresses, domains, URLs, and file hashes from configured notable event fields and queries supported intelligence providers, including VirusTotal, AbuseIPDB, MISP, and AlienVault OTX. Each provider operates independently. If one provider becomes unavailable or reaches its quota, enrichment continues through the remaining providers. Temporarily incomplete events can be retried when provider capacity becomes available again. Short Description:

Description:
PostHog activity logs record who did what in your PostHog organization. Every change to a feature flag, insight, dashboard, or other resource is captured, along with logins and account provisioning changes. This add-on collects that record into Splunk, so you can keep an audit trail alongside the rest of your security data, alert on sensitive changes, and meet compliance requirements. Splunk polls PostHog on a schedule you choose. There is nothing to run or host yourself, and the add-on works the same way on Splunk Cloud Platform and Splunk Enterprise. Events arrive in Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF) 1.5.0, so searches and dashboards that already understand OCSF work without a custom parser. Activity maps to three OCSF classes: Entity Management (3004) for changes to resources, Authentication (3002) for logins and logouts, and Account Change (3001) for provisioning. Activity types with no direct OCSF equivalent keep their original PostHog name, so nothing is dropped. Each poll resumes from where the previous one stopped, so entries are collected once. Every event carries the PostHog activity log ID in metadata.uid, which is stable across replays if you need to deduplicate. By default an event records which fields changed, not their values. That answers who changed what and when, which is what an audit trail needs. You can turn on changed values per input when you need the before and after content. Events are timestamped with when the activity happened in PostHog rather than when Splunk indexed them, so historical searches reflect real history. The add-on requires a PostHog personal API key with the activity_log:read scope. Activity logs are available on the PostHog Boost, Scale and Enterprise packages.
